prompt: You have not mentioned it before. Which is correct?

options.text: I am a university student.
options.why: Use "a" before a CONSONANT SOUND. "University" starts with a "yoo" sound, which is a consonant sound, so "a" is right even though the letter is a vowel.

options.text: I am an university student.
options.why: This follows the letter instead of the sound. The rule is about how the word is said, not how it is spelled.

options.text: I am university student.
options.why: A singular countable noun needs an article. Khmer has no articles, so this one is easy to drop.

options.text: I am the university student.
options.why: "The" points at one particular student both people already know about. Here you are saying what you are, so it must be "a".

hint: Say the word out loud. What sound starts it?

prompt: You have not mentioned it before. Which is correct?

options.text: She works as an engineer.
options.why: "Engineer" starts with a vowel sound, so it takes "an". The extra n just makes it easier to say.

options.text: She works as a engineer.
options.why: Two vowel sounds would collide. English puts an n between them.

options.text: She works as engineer.
options.why: A job title after "as" needs an article in English.

options.text: She works as the engineer.
options.why: "The" would mean one specific engineer already mentioned. This sentence is saying what her job is.

hint: a before a consonant sound, an before a vowel sound.

prompt: You have not mentioned it before. Which is correct?

options.text: I have three brothers.
options.why: English marks the plural on the NOUN as well as with the number. Both have to agree.

options.text: I have three brother.
options.why: Khmer does not add anything to the noun when a number is already there, so this carries over easily. English still needs the -s.

options.text: I have three brothers people.
options.why: "People" adds nothing. "Brothers" already says who they are.

options.text: I have the three brothers.
options.why: "The" would mean three particular brothers the reader already knows about. Introducing them for the first time needs no article here.

hint: The number is not enough on its own in English.

options.text: Last year I studied programming.
options.why: English marks past time on the VERB, even when a time word like "last year" is already there.

options.text: Last year I study programming.
options.why: Khmer leaves the verb alone and lets the time word do the work. English needs both.

options.text: Last year I am studying programming.
options.why: "Am" is present. You cannot mix a present verb with a finished past time.

options.text: Last year I have studied programming.
options.why: The present perfect cannot take a finished time like "last year". Use it for "I have studied programming for two years", with no end point.

hint: The time word does not excuse the verb.

options.text: He works at a bank.
options.why: With he, she or it in the present simple, the verb takes -s. It is the only place English still marks the person.

options.text: He work at a bank.
options.why: The -s is missing. This is the single most common slip for writers whose language does not change the verb.

options.text: He working at a bank.
options.why: "Working" needs a helper: "He is working". On its own it is not a finished verb.

options.text: He are working at a bank.
options.why: "Are" goes with you, we or they. With he it must be "is".

hint: he, she, it — add the s.

options.text: The list of students is on the desk.
options.why: The subject is "the list", which is singular. "Of students" only describes it, so the verb must agree with "list", not with the nearest word.

options.text: The list of students are on the desk.
options.why: This agrees with "students" because it sits next to the verb. The real subject is further back.

options.text: The list of student is on the desk.
options.why: The verb is right but "student" should be plural: a list of more than one.

options.text: The lists of students is on the desk.
options.why: Now the subject is plural, so the verb would have to be "are".

hint: Find the real subject. It is not always the nearest noun.

options.text: I do not have much time, but I have many ideas.
options.why: "Much" goes with things you cannot count, like time. "Many" goes with things you can, like ideas.

options.text: I do not have many time, but I have much ideas.
options.why: The two are swapped. Time cannot be counted one by one; ideas can.

options.text: I do not have much time, but I have much ideas.
options.why: The first half is right. "Much ideas" is wrong because ideas are countable.

options.text: I do not have much times, but I have many ideas.
options.why: "Much" never goes with a plural. "Times" is also the wrong word: it means occasions, as in "three times".

hint: Can you put a number in front of it?

options.text: There are many reasons for this.
options.why: The verb agrees with what COMES AFTER it. "Reasons" is plural, so it is "are".

options.text: There is many reasons for this.
options.why: "There" is not the subject. The thing that follows decides the verb, and "reasons" is plural.

options.text: There have many reasons for this.
options.why: "Have" is not used this way in English. The pattern is "there is" or "there are".

options.text: There is much reasons for this.
options.why: Two faults: "is" cannot go with a plural, and "much" never goes with a countable noun like reasons.

hint: Look at the word after the verb, not before it.

options.text: The company changed its name because it is growing.
options.why: "Its" with no apostrophe means belonging to it. "It is" with the apostrophe is short for it is. This sentence needs one of each.

options.text: The company changed it's name because its growing.
options.why: Both are the wrong way round. The test: if "it is" fits, use the apostrophe.

options.text: The company changed it's name because it is growing.
options.why: The first one is wrong. "The company changed it is name" makes no sense.

options.text: The company changed its name because its growing.
options.why: The second one is wrong. It should be "it is growing" or "it’s growing".

hint: Try reading it as "it is". Does the sentence still work?

options.text: They are proud of their work because they’re skilled.
options.why: "Their" shows belonging. "They’re" is short for they are. Each one is doing a different job here.

options.text: They are proud of there work because their skilled.
options.why: "There" means a place. It cannot show who something belongs to.

options.text: They are proud of they’re work because there skilled.
options.why: "They are work" makes no sense, which is the quick way to catch this one.

options.text: They are proud of their work because there skilled.
options.why: The first half is right. The second needs "they are", so "they’re".

hint: One means belonging, one means a place, one is two words squashed.

options.text: I like programming very much.
options.why: In English "very much" goes at the END, after the thing you like.

options.text: I very like programming.
options.why: This puts the intensifier before the verb, which is the order many other languages use. English does not allow it here.

options.text: I like very programming.
options.why: "Very" cannot sit directly in front of a noun like this.

options.text: Very I like programming.
options.why: Nothing in English starts a sentence this way.

hint: Where does "very much" go in an English sentence?

options.text: I am interested in software development.
options.why: "Interested" always takes "in". These pairings have to be learned one by one; no rule predicts them.

options.text: I am interested on software development.
options.why: "On" is used with other words, such as "focus on", but not with interested.

options.text: I am interested about software development.
options.why: "About" goes with words like curious or worried, not interested.

options.text: I am interested to software development.
options.why: "Interested to" only works before a verb, as in "interested to hear". Before a noun it is "in".

hint: This is one to memorise, not to work out.

options.text: She is good at mathematics.
options.why: "Good at" is the fixed pairing for a skill.

options.text: She is good in mathematics.
options.why: "Good in" is common in speech in some places but is not standard written English for a skill.

options.text: She is good on mathematics.
options.why: "On" is not used with good in this sense.

options.text: She is good of mathematics.
options.why: "Of" never follows "good" in this sense. No English pairing puts them together.

hint: Good ___ a skill.

options.text: I finished the project. It took three weeks.
options.why: These are two complete sentences, so they need a full stop between them, or a joining word such as "and".

options.text: I finished the project, it took three weeks.
options.why: A comma cannot join two complete sentences. This is a comma splice and it is one of the most heavily marked errors in exam writing.

options.text: I finished the project it took three weeks.
options.why: Nothing separates them at all, so the reader cannot tell where the first idea stops.

options.text: I finished the project, however it took three weeks.
options.why: “However” is not a joining word like “and”. It cannot hold two complete sentences together with only a comma. Write “I finished the project. However, it took three weeks.”

hint: Can each half stand alone as a sentence? Then a comma is not enough.

options.text: Because the deadline was short, we worked faster.
options.why: The "because" part leans on something, and the second half supplies it. Together they are complete.

options.text: Because the deadline was short.
options.why: "Because" opens a reason and then leaves the reader waiting. A reason on its own is a fragment.

options.text: Working faster every day.
options.why: There is no subject and no finished verb. "Working" needs a helper such as "we were".

options.text: Which we finished on time.
options.why: "Which" has to point back at something. On its own there is nothing for it to attach to.

hint: A sentence needs a subject, a verb, and no loose ends.

options.text: Python is easier to read than Java.
options.why: Short adjectives add -er. A "y" at the end becomes "i" first, giving easier.

options.text: Python is more easy to read than Java.
options.why: "More" is for longer adjectives, such as "more difficult". A two-syllable word ending in y takes -er.

options.text: Python is more easier to read than Java.
options.why: This marks the comparison twice. Use one or the other, never both.

options.text: Python is easier to read then Java.
options.why: "Then" means next in time. Comparison uses "than".

hint: Two ways to compare, and you may only use one.

options.text: I studied, then I rested. It was harder than I expected.
options.why: "Then" is about time, what happened next. "Than" is for comparing two things.

options.text: I studied, than I rested. It was harder then I expected.
options.why: Both are swapped. The two words sound almost the same but do completely different jobs.

options.text: I studied, then I rested. It was harder then I expected.
options.why: The first is right. The second is a comparison, so it needs "than".

options.text: I studied, than I rested. It was harder than I expected.
options.why: The second is right. The first is about time, so it needs "then".

hint: One has an A, and so does the word "compare".

prompt: Which is correct for one real future possibility?

options.text: If I pass the exam, I will study there.
options.why: For a real future possibility, English uses the PRESENT after "if" and "will" in the other half. The "if" half never takes will.

options.text: If I will pass the exam, I will study there.
options.why: "Will" is not used after "if" in this pattern, even though the meaning is about the future.

options.text: If I pass the exam, I study there.
options.why: This reads as a habit, something that happens every time, not a plan for one future event.

options.text: If I passed the exam, I will study there.
options.why: This mixes a past form with "will". For an unlikely case it would be "If I passed, I would study".

hint: Only one half of the sentence gets "will".

prompt: Which is the correct passive form of "The team built the app"?

options.text: The app was built by the team.
options.why: The passive is a form of "be" plus the past participle: was built. The thing that was acted on moves to the front.

options.text: The app was build by the team.
options.why: "Build" is the plain form. After "was" you need the past participle, "built".

options.text: The app is built by the team.
options.why: The original is past, so the passive must be past too.

options.text: The app has built by the team.
options.why: "Has built" is active and means the app did the building.

hint: A form of "be" plus the third form of the verb.

options.text: The developer who wrote this code is experienced.
options.why: "Who" is for people. "Which" is for things.

options.text: The developer which wrote this code is experienced.
options.why: "Which" is for things, not people.

options.text: The developer who he wrote this code is experienced.
options.why: "Who" is already the subject, so "he" repeats it. Only one subject is allowed.

options.text: The developer whom wrote this code is experienced.
options.why: "Whom" is for the object. Here the developer is doing the writing, so it is "who".

hint: People or things?

options.text: I am good at solving problems.
options.why: After a preposition such as "at", a verb always takes the -ing form.

options.text: I am good at solve problems.
options.why: The plain form cannot follow a preposition.

options.text: I am good at to solve problems.
options.why: Never put "to" plus a verb straight after a preposition.

options.text: I am good at solved problems.
options.why: The past form does not fit here. It would describe problems that were solved.

hint: What form follows at, in, on, of?

options.text: He gave me some useful advice.
options.why: "Advice" cannot be counted in English, so it takes no -s and no "an". To count it you say "a piece of advice".

options.text: He gave me some useful advices.
options.why: Advice has no plural form. This is a very common slip because many languages do count it.

options.text: He gave me an useful advice.
options.why: Two problems: advice takes no "a", and "useful" starts with a "yoo" sound so it would be "a" anyway.

options.text: He gave me a useful advices.
options.why: "A" and a plural cannot go together.

hint: Some English words simply have no plural. Information is another.

options.text: I want to join this programme. It will help my career.
options.why: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with a full stop. In a timed essay this is free marks.

options.text: i want to join this programme, it will help my career.
options.why: Two faults: neither sentence starts with a capital, and a comma cannot join two complete sentences.

options.text: I want to join this programme it will help my career.
options.why: No full stop between two complete sentences, so they run together.

options.text: I Want To Join This Programme.
options.why: Only the first word takes a capital, unless a word is a name.

hint: The easiest marks in the whole paper.

prompt: You want to add an opposite idea to your last sentence. Which word fits?

options.text: However
options.why: "However" signals that what follows goes against what came before. It is the clearest way to show a turn in your argument.

options.text: Therefore
options.why: "Therefore" introduces a RESULT of what came before, not an opposite.

options.text: Moreover
options.why: "Moreover" adds another point on the same side.

options.text: For example
options.why: That introduces an illustration of the same point, not a contrast.

hint: Which one turns the argument around?
